intro_band.agent_remit_summary: A self-hosted, single-tenant personal AI agent that runs one agent core across a CLI, a messaging gateway, a terminal UI and an Electron desktop app, with persistent memory, self-authored skills, cron automations and subagent delegation. It may use terminal, file, code-execution, web, browser, MCP, memory, skill, cron, delegation, voice, vision, image-generation and messaging-send tools, but only for the operator and callers on an operator-configured allowlist, and ingested content must always be treated as untrusted data. Destructive shell and file operations must be operator-approved in every execution context, credentials must be stripped from subprocesses and kept out of config.yaml, telemetry must be opt-in, and the desktop layer must render agent output as inert and must never install unverified runtime code.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: Two source roots: a Python agent (hermes-agent/) whose run_agent.py / agent/ loop dispatches tools registered in toolsets.py and tools/ — shell via tools/terminal_tool.py gated by the pattern-based tools/approval.py, MCP via tools/mcp_tool.py, and memory and skills via tools/memory_tool.py and tools/skill_manager_tool.py — plus a gateway (gateway/run.py, ~30 adapters in gateway/platforms/), an OpenAI-compatible API server, a FastAPI dashboard (hermes_cli/web_server.py) and the TUI JSON-RPC gateway. The Electron/TypeScript desktop app (hermes-desktop/) drives the agent over the loopback API server (src/main/hermes.ts), runs SSH tunnels and remote control (ssh-tunnel.ts, ssh-remote.ts), installs and updates the runtime by piping the upstream install.sh / install.ps1 from the main branch (src/main/installer.ts), and ships PostHog analytics in the renderer (src/renderer/src/utils/analytics.ts). The default terminal backend is the local host, and runtime state lives in ~/.hermes (config.yaml, .env, logs/, state.db, memories, skills).

behavior_summary:
Hermes has real, carefully built controls, but most of them are interactive-mode heuristics that quietly turn off at the edges. The approval gate prompts in the CLI and gateway, but the -z oneshot path forces HERMES_YOLO_MODE, other non-interactive contexts auto-approve with only a log warning, and write_file/patch overwrite files with no gate at all. The agent can also switch the gate off itself, because hermes config set approvals.mode off is not a flagged command. Gateway authorization is default-deny, yet the WeCom, Weixin and QQBot adapters default to dm_policy: open and short-circuit that check.

The dominant chain runs from untrusted content to host execution and persistence. Delimiter labeling covers only web, browser and MCP tool output, nothing enforces the documented rule that untrusted surfaces need a sandboxed backend (the default is local), and injected text can be written to MEMORY.md or to unscanned agent-created skills, where it is reloaded in every later session. On the desktop side, the runtime is installed by piping a script from a mutable main branch into a shell with no integrity check.

rules.rule_text: The agent MUST NOT act on instructions embedded in ingested content — web pages, emails, inbound messages, file contents, tool results, or MCP server responses — as though they were operator commands.
The agent MUST NOT grant itself new authority beyond what the operator has explicitly granted — new callers, egress destinations, tools, integrations, or trust tiers.
The agent MUST NOT disable, bypass, or route around its own safety controls (approval gate, output redaction, caller allowlists, credential scoping) in order to complete a task.

The desktop layer MUST NOT render agent-produced or tool-produced output as active or executable content; agent output MUST be treated as inert (displayed as data, never evaluated as HTML/script/markup with side effects).
MUST refuse to dispatch work, relay output, or resolve approvals until an operator-configured allowlist is set. MUST NOT fail open when no allowlist is configured.
MUST default to a loopback bind; MUST require an allowlist before serving.
MUST bind loopback only and rely on OS-level access control; MUST NOT be exposed beyond the local user without an explicit network authentication layer.

Enabled-surface closure: the set of enabled messaging channels and network-exposed HTTP surfaces (API server, dashboard, plugins) is operator-configured; any channel or surface not enabled by the operator is unauthorized by default, and one found active outside that configured set is a trust-expansion finding.
Trusted People / Accounts

Any outbound destination reached in code but absent from the operator's configured/allowlisted set is a trust expansion; under egress isolation, outbound connections MUST be limited to the allowlisted hosts.

Third-party MCP servers, skills, and plugins — but each MUST be reviewed and approved by the operator before install or activation; none may be auto-trusted on the strength of its own description alone.
Unreviewed third-party skills, plugins, or MCP servers (per the operator-review requirement in Trusted Services / Integrations).
Callers outside the configured authorization set (see Trusted People / Accounts).

rules.section: Tools and Capabilities > Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)
rules.rule_text: Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)

rules.section: Tools and Capabilities > Restricted Tools (Require Approval Before Use)
rules.rule_text: Authorized isolation posture (closure): the default local (host) terminal backend is authorized only for trusted content; any untrusted input surface MUST run under a sandboxed terminal backend (Docker/Modal/Daytona) or whole-process wrapping.
Allowed Data Sources

Provider API keys and gateway/platform tokens MUST NOT be passed into lower-trust in-process or subprocess components (shell subprocesses, the code-execution child, MCP subprocesses, cron job scripts); they MUST be stripped from that environment by default, and the strip set MUST cover every configured provider/gateway credential (a registry-derived denylist is acceptable).
Credentials MUST NOT be written into the main config file or into version control; they belong in the operator credential file with tight permissions (or a dedicated secret store).

Operator credentials and session authorization material MUST NOT egress to any destination outside the trust envelope, whether via environment leakage, adapter logging, or a transport error that flushes them upstream.
Outbound telemetry and usage attribution are opt-in and off by default; no telemetry or usage data may egress unless the operator has explicitly enabled it.
Allowed Without Approval

rules.section: Action Boundaries > Requires Human Approval Before Execution > Agent core
rules.rule_text: Destructive or irreversible shell and file operations (deletion, overwrite, bulk or recursive changes) MUST require operator approval before execution, in every execution context and regardless of interactive vs. unattended mode.

rules.section: Action Boundaries > Requires Human Approval Before Execution > Agent core
rules.rule_text: Binding a local-only surface (dashboard, plugin HTTP server, or any local-IPC surface) to a non-loopback interface MUST be an explicit operator decision, never taken autonomously.

rules.section: Action Boundaries > Never Allowed > Agent core
rules.rule_text: Agent work MUST NOT be dispatched, output relayed, or approvals resolved for any caller outside the configured authorization set.

rules.section: Action Boundaries > Never Allowed > Desktop layer
rules.rule_text: The desktop self-update and first-run install path MUST NOT fetch or install agent runtime code from an unverified or unauthenticated source; installers and runtime updates MUST be integrity-verified before they replace the running app or backend.

rules.section: Escalation Rules > Halt Agent and Alert Operator
rules.rule_text: On a destructive-command match, the response MUST be halt-pending-approval — pause and prompt the operator, never autonomous execution (the runtime enforcement of the destructive-operation approval gate).

rules.section: Escalation Rules > Halt Agent and Alert Operator
rules.rule_text: On an enabled network-exposed adapter with no caller allowlist, the response MUST be fail-closed — refuse to serve rather than dispatch.

rules.section: Escalation Rules > Alert Operator (Do Not Halt)
rules.rule_text: When Skills Guard detects injection-like patterns in installable skill or plugin content, surface the detection to the operator for review before install.

rules.section: Escalation Rules > Alert Operator (Do Not Halt)
rules.rule_text: When output redaction detects a secret-like pattern in agent output, strip it from display and continue.

Tool invocations, approval decisions, and session lifecycle events MUST be recorded to durable, structured logs (`agent.log` / `gateway.log`; `desktop.log` for the desktop layer) sufficient to reconstruct what the agent did.

findings.summary: Destructive-operation approval disappears outside the interactive CLI and gateway: oneshot mode forces yolo, other unattended contexts auto-approve, and file-tool overwrites are never gated.
findings.description: The remit requires approval for destructive shell and file operations in every execution context, but hermes -z sets HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1 unconditionally, and any context that is not CLI, gateway or cron silently auto-approves a matched dangerous command, logging only a warning. write_file and patch overwrite arbitrary files outside a small system-path list with no approval at all, so an injected or hallucinated destructive action runs unattended on the host.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Without Approval

Destructive or irreversible shell and file operations (deletion, overwrite, bulk or recursive changes) MUST require operator approval before execution, in every execution context and regardless of interactive vs. unattended mode.

On a destructive-command match, the response MUST be halt-pending-approval — pause and prompt the operator, never autonomous execution (the runtime enforcement of the destructive-operation approval gate).

evidence.snippet: oneshot (-z) mode sets os.environ["HERMES_YOLO_MODE"] = "1" and HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1 for every call, so _YOLO_MODE_FROZEN bypasses all dangerous-command approval (module docstring: "Approvals = auto-bypassed")

check_dangerous_command, lines 966-988 — when neither HERMES_INTERACTIVE nor a gateway context is set and the session is not cron-deny, logs "AUTO-APPROVED dangerous command in non-interactive non-gateway context" and returns approved; check_all_command_guards (1200-1223) and check_execute_code_guard (1491-1511) do the same, and container backends skip the gate entirely (940)

recommended_actions: In tools/approval.py, make the non-interactive, non-gateway branch deny dangerous matches by default (mirroring approvals.cron_mode: deny), and in hermes_cli/oneshot.py drop the forced HERMES_YOLO_MODE in favour of an explicit --yolo flag the operator must pass.

Route write_file/patch overwrites of existing files outside the working directory through the same approval decision as shell writes, rather than relying only on the /etc-prefix check in tools/file_tools.py.

findings.summary: Untrusted web, email, file and MCP content reaches a host shell on the default local backend and can persist into memory or agent-authored skills, with only partial, prompt-level labeling.
findings.description: Chain: (1) only web_*, browser_* and mcp_* results get untrusted_tool_result delimiters, a model-obedience control whose closing tag is not escaped, while read_file, terminal output and email bodies arrive unlabeled. (2) The terminal backend defaults to local, nothing rejects an untrusted ingress surface on it, and commands that do not match the approval denylist run on the host without a prompt. (3) The memory tool writes MEMORY.md/USER.md after only a regex threat scan, and agent-created skills are not scanned at all by default, so an injected instruction is reloaded into every later session.
policy_rule_text: The agent MUST NOT act on instructions embedded in ingested content — web pages, emails, inbound messages, file contents, tool results, or MCP server responses — as though they were operator commands.

Authorized isolation posture (closure): the default local (host) terminal backend is authorized only for trusted content; any untrusted input surface MUST run under a sandboxed terminal backend (Docker/Modal/Daytona) or whole-process wrapping.

evidence.snippet: _UNTRUSTED_TOOL_NAMES = {web_extract, web_search} plus prefixes browser_ and mcp_ (lines 351-397); every other tool result, including read_file, terminal, session_search and inbound email text, is passed to the model without provenance labeling, and wrapped content is not escaped for a literal closing delimiter

terminal.backend defaults to "local" (host execution); there is no code path that refuses or warns when web, email or MCP ingress is enabled on the local backend, and skills.guard_agent_created defaults to False (line 1555), so agent-authored skills skip Skills Guard; memory_tool.py:304 accepts memory writes after a regex scan only, and they are reloaded at every session start

recommended_actions: Enforce the remit's isolation posture in code: at gateway and agent start, refuse (or require an explicit break-glass flag for) enabling email, web-fetch, browser or third-party MCP ingress while terminal.backend is local.

Extend _maybe_wrap_untrusted to all content-returning tools (file reads, terminal output, inbound gateway text), escape the closing delimiter, and default skills.guard_agent_created to true with operator review of memory writes that originate in a turn containing untrusted content.

findings.summary: The WeCom, Weixin and QQBot adapters default to dm_policy "open" and claim to enforce their own access policy, so the gateway's default-deny is skipped and any sender can dispatch agent work.
findings.description: _is_user_authorized returns True whenever no env allowlist is set and the adapter reports enforces_own_access_policy. These three adapters set that flag to True while their intake check _is_dm_allowed returns True for the default "open" policy. An enabled adapter with no allowlist therefore fails open, giving any platform user a terminal-capable agent: the exact condition the remit and SECURITY.md §2.6 call an in-scope bug.
policy_rule_text: MUST refuse to dispatch work, relay output, or resolve approvals until an operator-configured allowlist is set. MUST NOT fail open when no allowlist is configured.
Agent work MUST NOT be dispatched, output relayed, or approvals resolved for any caller outside the configured authorization set.
On an enabled network-exposed adapter with no caller allowlist, the response MUST be fail-closed — refuse to serve rather than dispatch.

evidence.snippet: _is_user_authorized, lines 6745-6758 — when no platform, group or global allowlist is set, "if self._adapter_enforces_own_access_policy(source.platform): return True" runs before the GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS default-deny

self._dm_policy = ... os.getenv("WEIXIN_DM_POLICY", "open"); _is_dm_allowed (1444-1449) returns True unless the policy is "disabled" or "allowlist", and enforces_own_access_policy returns True (1452); WeCom (wecom.py:163, 851-860) and QQBot (qqbot/adapter.py:211, 273) follow the same pattern

recommended_actions: Change the default dm_policy/group_policy for WeCom, Weixin and QQBot to allowlist (or pairing), and have connect() refuse to start when the policy is open and no explicit allow-all flag is set.
In gateway/run.py, honour enforces_own_access_policy only when the adapter reports a non-open policy, so the gateway's default-deny remains the backstop.

findings.summary: The desktop first-run installer pipes install.sh/install.ps1 from the mutable main branch into a shell with no hash or signature check, and Windows/Linux app builds are unsigned.
findings.description: The remit forbids installing runtime code from an unverified source and requires integrity verification before replacement. installer.ts runs curl -fsSL …/main/scripts/install.sh | bash, and the PowerShell path does the same with install.ps1, so whatever the branch head serves, including its downstream clone and dependency install, executes as the user. electron-builder.yml notarizes only macOS; Windows NSIS/portable and Linux AppImage updates carry no publisher signature (the README tells users to bypass SmartScreen and use --nogpgcheck).
policy_rule_text: The desktop self-update and first-run install path MUST NOT fetch or install agent runtime code from an unverified or unauthenticated source; installers and runtime updates MUST be integrity-verified before they replace the running app or backend.

evidence.snippet: installCmd = "curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --skip-setup", spawned via bash -c; the Windows wrapper (lines 1001-1012) downloads .../main/scripts/install.ps1 with Invoke-WebRequest and executes it; no checksum, pinned ref or signature is checked on either path

mac sets hardenedRuntime and notarize: true, but the win (nsis, portable) and linux (AppImage, snap, deb, rpm) targets have no signing configuration; electron-updater publishes from the fathah/hermes-desktop GitHub releases

recommended_actions: Pin the installer to a release tag and verify a published SHA-256 (or a minisign/Sigstore signature) of install.sh/install.ps1 in installer.ts before executing them, rather than piping main into a shell.
Sign the Windows builds (and set publisherName so electron-updater verifies the signature) and sign the Linux packages before enabling in-place updates.

findings.summary: The agent can turn off its own approval gate by running hermes config set approvals.mode off through the terminal tool, a command the denylist does not flag.
findings.description: File tools correctly write-deny config.yaml, but the shell path is open. set_config_value writes any non-credential key into config.yaml with no protected-key check, and the only hermes subcommands in DANGEROUS_PATTERNS are gateway stop/restart and update. Because _get_approval_mode() re-reads config on every check, a single unprompted command (or a similar edit to approvals.cron_mode) persistently removes the remit's halt-pending-approval control for every later action.
policy_rule_text: The agent MUST NOT grant itself new authority beyond what the operator has explicitly granted — new callers, egress destinations, tools, integrations, or trust tiers.
The agent MUST NOT disable, bypass, or route around its own safety controls (approval gate, output redaction, caller allowlists, credential scoping) in order to complete a task.

evidence.snippet: set_config_value(key, value) routes any key not ending in _API_KEY/_TOKEN into config.yaml via nested-key set, with no denylist for approvals.*, security.* or allowlist keys

the hermes-specific DANGEROUS_PATTERNS cover only "hermes gateway stop/restart" and "hermes update" (368-369), so "hermes config set approvals.mode off" passes detect_dangerous_command; check_all_command_guards then returns approved for every command once approval_mode == "off" (line 1197)

recommended_actions: Add a DANGEROUS_PATTERNS entry (or a hardline rule) for hermes config set / hermes config edit against approvals.*, security.*, skills.guard_* and allowlist keys, and make set_config_value refuse those keys when HERMES_SESSION_* or HERMES_GATEWAY_SESSION indicates an agent-spawned process.
Snapshot the approval mode at session start and require an operator action (slash command or restart), not a mid-session config re-read, to lower it.

findings.summary: The email adapter takes caller identity from the unauthenticated From header, so anyone who spoofs an allowlisted operator address can dispatch agent work.
findings.description: EMAIL_ALLOWED_USERS is checked against user_id, which is just the parsed From: address. No DKIM, SPF/DMARC or Authentication-Results verification happens before the message becomes a MessageEvent. Because the allowlist is the remit's sole authorization boundary for messaging callers, a forged sender passes as the operator and drives a terminal-capable agent.
policy_rule_text: Trusted People / Accounts
Callers outside the configured authorization set (see Trusted People / Accounts).

evidence.snippet: sender_raw = msg.get("From", ""); sender_addr = _extract_email_address(sender_raw) — the only authentication-relevant check before dispatch is _is_automated_sender (noreply filtering)
build_source(chat_id=sender_addr, user_id=sender_addr, ...) — the unverified header address becomes the identity that gateway/run.py _is_user_authorized compares against EMAIL_ALLOWED_USERS

recommended_actions: In gateway/platforms/email.py, parse the receiving server's Authentication-Results header and require dkim=pass aligned with the From domain (or dmarc=pass) before building the source; drop or quarantine messages that fail.
Document email as an untrusted surface that requires the sandboxed posture, and offer a shared-secret subject tag or pairing step as a second factor for allowlisted senders.

findings.summary: The terminal subprocess credential denylist misses several gateway secrets (WeCom, Weixin, DingTalk, Feishu, LINE, Teams), so those tokens are inherited by every shell command.
findings.description: _build_provider_env_blocklist() derives the strip set from PROVIDER_REGISTRY, from OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS entries in the tool/messaging categories, and from a hand-written list. Secrets registered only in _EXTRA_ENV_KEYS or in plugin plugin.yaml manifests are never added. Because the terminal path is a denylist (pass unless blocked), unlike the MCP allowlist and the execute_code substring scrub, these credentials are readable by any LLM-emitted command and can egress through it, contrary to the remit's every-credential strip requirement.
policy_rule_text: Provider API keys and gateway/platform tokens MUST NOT be passed into lower-trust in-process or subprocess components (shell subprocesses, the code-execution child, MCP subprocesses, cron job scripts); they MUST be stripped from that environment by default, and the strip set MUST cover every configured provider/gateway credential (a registry-derived denylist is acceptable).

Operator credentials and session authorization material MUST NOT egress to any destination outside the trust envelope, whether via environment leakage, adapter logging, or a transport error that flushes them upstream.

evidence.snippet: blocklist adds OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS names only when category in {"tool", "messaging"} (lines 115-121) and _sanitize_subprocess_env (205-224) keeps every key not in that blocklist

DINGTALK_CLIENT_SECRET, FEISHU_APP_SECRET, WECOM_SECRET, WECOM_CALLBACK_CORP_SECRET, WECOM_CALLBACK_ENCODING_AES_KEY and WEIXIN_TOKEN appear only in _EXTRA_ENV_KEYS (lines 186-196) with no OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS entry; plugin secrets LINE_CHANNEL_SECRET/TEAMS_CLIENT_SECRET are declared only in plugins/platforms/*/plugin.yaml

recommended_actions: Build the terminal strip set from every declared credential source: _EXTRA_ENV_KEYS entries matching secret-like names, plugin-manifest secret: true env declarations, and custom_providers[*].key_env.
Better still, switch _sanitize_subprocess_env to the same allowlist-plus-passthrough model already used for MCP (tools/mcp_tool.py _build_safe_env), so new credentials are stripped by default.

findings.summary: MCP servers can add or redefine tools mid-session through tools/list_changed with no operator review, and descriptions that trip the injection scan are only logged, not blocked.
findings.description: The remit requires each integration to be operator-reviewed before activation, and forbids auto-trusting one on the strength of its own description. On a tools/list_changed notification, _refresh_tools re-registers whatever the server now advertises, and _scan_mcp_description only emits a warning, so a rug-pulled or poisoned tool definition goes straight into the model's tool schema. Server-initiated sampling (sampling/createMessage) is also enabled by default for every configured server.

tags.label: Tool definitions are signed and version-pinned

policy_rule_text: Third-party MCP servers, skills, and plugins — but each MUST be reviewed and approved by the operator before install or activation; none may be auto-trusted on the strength of its own description alone.
Unreviewed third-party skills, plugins, or MCP servers (per the operator-review requirement in Trusted Services / Integrations).

evidence.snippet: _refresh_tools (1215-1250), triggered by notifications/tools/list_changed — fetches list_tools() and re-registers every tool through _register_server_tools with no diff approval, pin or signature check; it only logs added/removed names

_scan_mcp_description — "These are WARNING-level — we log but don't block" (341-342); matched descriptions are still registered, and sampling_config.get("enabled", True) at line 1673 turns sampling on by default

recommended_actions: Pin each server's tool set at first operator approval (name plus description hash) and, on tools/list_changed, quarantine new or changed tools until the operator approves the diff, rather than re-registering automatically.
Refuse to register tools whose description matches _MCP_INJECTION_PATTERNS unless the operator allowlists them, and default mcp_servers.NAME.sampling.enabled to false.

findings.summary: The custom-endpoint setup flows write the operator's API key in plaintext into config.yaml instead of the credential file.
findings.description: The remit says credentials must never be written into the main config file, and SECURITY.md §4 says the same. hermes model's custom-endpoint flow sets model.api_key, _save_custom_provider stores api_key in custom_providers, and the auxiliary-model flow writes auxiliary.TASK.api_key. All of these are saved through save_config to config.yaml, a file operators routinely share, back up and version.
policy_rule_text: Credentials MUST NOT be written into the main config file or into version control; they belong in the operator credential file with tight permissions (or a dedicated secret store).

evidence.snippet: _model_flow_custom — model["provider"] = "custom"; model["base_url"] = effective_url; if effective_key: model["api_key"] = effective_key; save_config(cfg)

_save_custom_provider builds entry = {"name", "base_url"} and sets entry["api_key"] = api_key before writing cfg["custom_providers"]; _save_aux_choice (line 2713) likewise persists entry["api_key"] under auxiliary.TASK

recommended_actions: Store custom-endpoint keys in ~/.hermes/.env via save_env_value under a generated name and persist only key_env in config.yaml; migrate existing inline api_key values on load.
Register each generated key_env in the subprocess strip set (see PRAX-2026-10-19-007).

findings.summary: Desktop PostHog analytics are on by default in official builds: consent defaults to enabled whenever a build-time key is present, which the release workflow always injects.
findings.description: The remit requires telemetry to be opt-in and off by default. isAnalyticsEnabled() returns hasKey on first run, and release.yml bakes VITE_POSTHOG_KEY into the macOS and Linux builds, so screen views, feature usage and an anonymous ID go to a third-party host the operator never configured. The renderer CSP's default-src 'self' may incidentally block the requests, but that is a side effect rather than a control, which is why confidence is Medium.
policy_rule_text: Outbound telemetry and usage attribution are opt-in and off by default; no telemetry or usage data may egress unless the operator has explicitly enabled it.

Any outbound destination reached in code but absent from the operator's configured/allowlisted set is a trust expansion; under egress isolation, outbound connections MUST be limited to the allowlisted hosts.

evidence.snippet: isAnalyticsEnabled() — "Default to true for official builds (key present)"; if localStorage consent is null, returns hasKey; initAnalytics() then calls posthog.init with the eu.i.posthog.com default host
VITE_POSTHOG_KEY and VITE_POSTHOG_HOST are injected from repository secrets into the release build steps (also line 160)

recommended_actions: In analytics.ts, return false when no consent is stored, and add an explicit opt-in prompt to onboarding before initAnalytics() runs.
Record the consent decision in the desktop settings UI and log it, so operators can verify that no telemetry egresses without their choice.

findings.summary: Webhook-style HTTP receivers (generic webhook, WeCom callback, MS Graph webhook, LINE, Teams) bind 0.0.0.0 by default instead of the loopback default the remit requires.
findings.description: The API server and dashboard default to 127.0.0.1, but the callback receivers default to all interfaces, and Teams hard-codes 0.0.0.0 with no host option. These routes carry per-platform signature or HMAC checks and bypass the caller allowlist by design, so the exposure is authenticated. They still widen the network surface without an explicit operator choice, and any signature-validation bug is directly internet-reachable.
policy_rule_text: MUST default to a loopback bind; MUST require an allowlist before serving.

evidence.snippet: DEFAULT_HOST = "0.0.0.0" (also wecom_callback.py:54, msgraph_webhook.py:33, gateway/config.py:1663 WECOM_CALLBACK_HOST default, plugins/platforms/line/adapter.py:646)
site = web.TCPSite(self._runner, "0.0.0.0", self._port) — the bind address is hard-coded and not configurable

recommended_actions: Default every callback receiver to 127.0.0.1 (operators front them with a tunnel or reverse proxy) and require an explicit host: setting to listen publicly, logging a startup warning when it does.
Make the Teams adapter honour a configurable host like the other adapters.

findings.summary: Approval decisions are not written to any durable log, and tool invocations reach agent.log only at DEBUG, so the structured audit trail the remit requires is incomplete.
findings.description: agent.log is INFO+ free text. conversation_loop.py logs each tool call at DEBUG, so it is dropped by default, and operator approve or deny outcomes are surfaced only through plugin hooks (post_approval_response) and the in-memory session set. state.db keeps tool calls with timestamps, but not who approved what, so an approval incident cannot be reconstructed from Hermes' own records.
policy_rule_text: Tool invocations, approval decisions, and session lifecycle events MUST be recorded to durable, structured logs (`agent.log` / `gateway.log`; `desktop.log` for the desktop layer) sufficient to reconstruct what the agent did.

evidence.snippet: the CLI approval path (and the gateway path at line 1149) fires _fire_approval_hook("post_approval_response", ..., choice=choice) and returns; there is no logger.info or persisted record of the approve/deny decision (logger calls in approval.py are warnings for hardline/auto-approve only)
logging.debug(f"Tool call: {tc.function.name} with args: ...") — tool invocations are emitted below the INFO threshold of agent.log configured in hermes_logging.py:215-222

recommended_actions: Emit one structured (JSON) INFO record per tool invocation and per approval decision (session, surface, pattern key, choice, approver) to agent.log/gateway.log, or add an approvals table to state.db.
Add a JSON formatter option to hermes_logging.py so these records can feed automated detection.

findings.summary: The shared core toolset registers computer_use (macOS GUI control) and Home Assistant ha_call_service (physical device actuation), neither of which is in the remit's Known Good Baseline.
findings.description: Under the remit's Allowed Tools closure, any capability outside the baseline is unauthorized. _HERMES_CORE_TOOLS is shared by the CLI and every messaging platform, and it includes computer_use plus four ha_* tools. These activate automatically once their prerequisite (cua-driver installed, HASS_TOKEN set) is present, with no separate operator authorization tied to the remit.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)

evidence.snippet: _HERMES_CORE_TOOLS includes "ha_list_entities", "ha_get_state", "ha_list_services", "ha_call_service" (gated on HASS_TOKEN via check_fn) and, at line 72, "computer_use" (gated on cua-driver being installed via check_fn)

recommended_actions: Move computer_use and ha_call_service out of _HERMES_CORE_TOOLS into opt-in toolsets that must be named explicitly in platform_toolsets, or add them to the remit's baseline if the operator intends them.

findings.summary: The Nous-approved n8n MCP catalog entry installs a third-party repo at the floating ref main and bootstraps unpinned requirements, contradicting the manifest's own pin requirement.
findings.description: The manifest states "Pin to a commit/tag. Required — manifests do not float HEAD", yet it sets ref: main for CyberSamuraiX/hermes-n8n-mcp. Its bootstrap runs pip install -r requirements.txt from that moving checkout, so a later upstream push changes the code and dependencies that hermes mcp install official/n8n executes under the catalog's approval.

tags.label: Dependencies pinned and scanned for CVEs

evidence.snippet: install.type git, url https://github.com/CyberSamuraiX/hermes-n8n-mcp.git, comment "Pin to a commit/tag. Required — manifests do not float HEAD." directly above "ref: main"; bootstrap runs ".venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt"

recommended_actions: Replace ref: main with a reviewed commit SHA, and add a CI check in the catalog path that rejects branch-name refs in optional-mcps/*/manifest.yaml.

findings.summary: The desktop app's runtime dependencies, including electron-updater and posthog-js, are caret-ranged, and the desktop repo has no dependency or vulnerability scanning.
findings.description: The agent repo exact-pins every Python dependency after a supply-chain incident, but hermes-desktop/package.json uses ^ ranges for all runtime deps. A committed package-lock.json and npm ci in CI keep builds reproducible, but no Dependabot, osv-scanner or npm audit step exists in .github/workflows, so lockfile refreshes pull new versions with no review.

evidence.snippet: dependencies use caret ranges — electron-updater ^6.3.9, posthog-js ^1.376.0, better-sqlite3 ^12.8.0, react-markdown ^10.1.0, and the rest
ci.yml runs npm ci, typecheck, test and a non-gating lint only; neither ci.yml nor release.yml has a dependency or vulnerability scan, and hermes-desktop/.github has no dependabot.yml

recommended_actions: Pin the desktop runtime dependencies exactly (matching the agent's policy) and add Dependabot plus an osv-scanner or npm audit --omit=dev job to hermes-desktop/.github/workflows/ci.yml.

positives.title: API server fails closed without a key
positives.description: The API server adapter refuses to start unless API_SERVER_KEY is set, even on loopback, and refuses placeholder keys on network-accessible binds. Its default host is 127.0.0.1.

positives.title: Dashboard loopback, Host-header and token gates
positives.description: The dashboard binds loopback by default, checks the Host header against DNS rebinding, requires a per-process session token on REST and WebSocket, and needs --insecure plus an OAuth gate for non-loopback binds.

positives.title: Default-deny gateway authorization
positives.description: _is_user_authorized denies any caller who is not on an env allowlist, a pairing list or an explicit allow-all flag, and the gateway warns at startup when no allowlists are configured.

positives.title: Hardline command floor and cron deny default
positives.description: Catastrophic commands (rm -rf /, mkfs, dd to raw devices, fork bombs, shutdown) are blocked before any yolo or mode=off bypass, and cron jobs deny dangerous commands unless the operator opts in.

positives.title: MCP subprocess environment allowlist
positives.description: MCP stdio servers receive only an allowlisted set of OS variables plus their explicitly configured env, so provider and gateway credentials do not reach them by default.

positives.title: Inert agent-output rendering in the desktop renderer
positives.description: Agent markdown is rendered with react-markdown and no raw-HTML plugin, under a strict CSP (script-src 'self', img-src 'self' data:), with sandboxed, context-isolated renderers and a protocol allowlist for opened links.

positives.title: Exact-pinned Python dependencies with OSV CI
positives.description: Every core and lazy-installed Python dependency is pinned with == and locked in uv.lock, and osv-scanner runs on PR, push and a weekly schedule alongside a supply-chain-audit workflow and Dependabot.

positives.title: Security regression tests tied to fixed bypasses
positives.description: Reported authorization and injection bypasses are fixed and pinned with regression tests that cite the originating issue, and those tests run in CI on every PR. This is evidence of a working feedback loop.

positives.title: Contained attachment cache paths
positives.description: Inbound document filenames are reduced to their basename and resolve-checked against the cache directory before any write, which closes the external-filename path-traversal pattern.

positives.title: Webhook routes require HMAC secrets
positives.description: The generic webhook adapter refuses routes without an HMAC secret and allows its INSECURE_NO_AUTH testing escape hatch only on loopback hosts.

WARNING+ errors, including auto-approved dangerous-command and hardline-block warnings

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Partial. Hermes has operative controls in every RAISE category: an approval gate with a hardline floor, default-deny gateway authorization, a fail-closed API server, subprocess credential scrubbing, exact-pinned Python dependencies with OSV scanning, a security regression suite tied to fixed bypasses, and structured session storage. In each category, though, a key path is left open: the approval gate is missing or self-disableable in non-interactive contexts, external content is only partly labeled and reaches a host shell by default, three adapters fail open, and the desktop installs unverified runtime code. Neither the red-team practice nor the monitoring extends to a dedicated adversarial corpus or to alerting.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The remit itself scopes a general-purpose personal agent. Code-level gates exist (per-platform toolsets, check_fn capability gating, and a constrained webhook-safe toolset in toolsets.py), but the shared core list registers computer_use and Home Assistant ha_call_service, which lie outside the remit's baseline (PRAX-2026-10-19-013), so domain enforcement is partial.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: The dominant path is tool results, and it is covered only by code-inserted delimiters that depend on the model obeying them. They apply to web, browser and MCP tools only (agent/tool_dispatch_helpers.py); file, terminal and email content enters unlabeled. Memory and context-file threat scans are heuristics, and agent-created skills are unscanned by default, so the ladder caps this category at 2 (PRAX-2026-10-19-002).

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Real controls run on the main path: the approval gate with a hardline floor in CLI, gateway and TUI; cron approvals defaulting to deny; an API server that refuses to start without a key; dashboard host and token gates; default-deny gateway authorization; and env scrubbing. However, the gate is bypassed in oneshot and non-interactive contexts and for file overwrites (001) and can be disabled by the agent with an unflagged hermes config set (005), three adapters fail open (003), email trusts the From header (006), and external content reaches the host shell unsanitized (002), which caps the category at 2.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: The agent side is strong: exact == pins plus uv.lock, exact-pinned lazy deps, osv-scanner on PR, push and a weekly schedule, supply-chain-audit, Dependabot, and the MCP OSV malware check (M11). The combined subject, however, installs its runtime with an unverified curl | bash from main and ships unsigned Windows/Linux builds (004), lets MCP tools change at runtime without review (008), floats the n8n catalog ref (014), uses caret-ranged desktop deps (015) and has no SBOM (M10: none). Bands 2 and 3 are both defensible, so the lower is chosen.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: M1 found 106 security-named tests, including regression tests that cite fixed bypass issues (#17775 busy-session auth, #3968 cron injection, #24457 fail-closed), and they run on every PR and push (M6, M7). M9 links the promptware defense and a GHSA filter to PRs, so a findings-to-fixes feedback loop exists. M2 (adversarial corpus), M3 (adversarial tooling), M5 (dated reports) and M8 (gating) are all none, so the call between 2 and 3 resolves to the lower band; practice kept outside the repo could raise it.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: hermes_logging.py writes rotating, redacted agent.log, errors.log and gateway.log, and state.db keeps timestamped tool calls per session, which together give a durable action record. However, the log lines are free text, tool invocations are logged only at DEBUG, approval decisions are not logged (PRAX-2026-10-19-012), and M12 found no external telemetry or alerting, so the category stays at 2.
